artists.biography:
The Mute Gods are a German and English band uniting Nick Beggs, Marco Minnemann and Roger King.  
Beggs approached King — with whom he had worked as part of Steve Hackett's band — about a collaboration in 2014, and Minnemann was chosen as the drummer after Beggs had toured with him as part of Steven Wilson's band.

Their first album, Do Nothing till You Hear from Me is planned for release on 22 January 2016. Beggs wrote the majority of the album on tour in 2014, and has described it as "a rather disgruntled rant at the dystopia we've created for ourselves and our children". In addition to Minnemann, the album features some guest drummers, including Nick D'Virgilio and Gary O'Toole. In November 2015, the band released two videos — one of which being a 360 degree video — for the album's title track. According to Nick Beggs, "Do Nothing till You Hear from Me" was inspired by Dwight D. Eisenhower's warning about the potential rise of the military–industrial complex, as well as the geologist Phil Schneider, who made several claims regarding UFOs, before dying under mysterious circumstances.

Band members:

    Nick Beggs – bass guitars, Chapman Stick, guitars, vocals
    Roger King – keyboards, production
    Marco Minnemann – drums, guitars, sound modelling
 .

perplexity.description:
Tardigrades Will Inherit The Earth is the second studio album by the English progressive rock supergroup The Mute Gods, released in 2017 on Inside Out Music. The band, featuring Nick Beggs, Marco Minnemann, and Roger King, delivers a dynamic blend of progressive rock and crossover prog, marked by intricate musicianship, socially conscious lyrics, and a fusion of melodic and aggressive elements. The album’s sound is characterized by complex rhythms, layered instrumentation, and a balance between atmospheric passages and driving rock sections, reflecting the group’s collective experience in the progressive rock scene.

Following their debut Do Nothing till You Hear from Me, Tardigrades Will Inherit The Earth further established The Mute Gods’ reputation for combining political and philosophical themes with sophisticated musical arrangements. The album was well-received by critics, who praised its energy, lyrical depth, and the band’s technical prowess. It solidified the group’s place in the modern progressive rock landscape and was noted for its urgent, sometimes confrontational tone, aligning with the band’s reputation for addressing contemporary societal issues through their music.
